newsitem.title: FRANCE: French hospital doctors extend strike, plan march.
newsitem.headline: French hospital doctors extend strike, plan march.

text.p: A strike by junior hospital doctors protesting against reform of France's generous medical system was extended on Thursday to include most teaching hospitals and strike leaders called for a national protest on Sunday.
The widening action which was launched on March 11 is a challenge to the conservative government's plans to brake spending on healthcare.

The government has made some concessions but it can ill afford to give in to the student doctors since reducing the health fund deficit is a key part of French efforts to qualify for a planned single European Union currency, which is set to start on January 1, 1999.
Labour and Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot, after making several concessions last week, has pledged to stand firm against the rest of the strikers' demands.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said in a television interview on Thursday that the government would make a big effort to explain its reforms to the strikers since much information about it was wrong.
Public health care spending is the leading factor in France's welfare deficit, expected to show a shortfall of about 33 billion francs ($5.8 billion) this year after 51.6 billion francs last year.
The stoppage has reduced service to a bare minimum in 15 of the country's 26 teaching hospitals, the medical students' union said. Emergency care at all hospitals is guaranteed.
The strikers have been joined by some clinic directors and supported by three unions representing mostly specialist doctors in private practice.
But the largest general practitioners' union, MG France, opposes the strike and supports the reform plan.
The strike was sparked by plans to fine doctors who overshoot government-set limits on medical costs.
The reforms would also impose compliance with enforceable medical standards, mandate continuous doctor training and make a personal health card compulsory for all patients.
The specialist doctors' unions say the changes will make them pay between 6,000 and 100,000 francs if national health costs go over budget in 1997.
The plan challenges the previously almost total freedom of French doctors to consult and prescribe as they wish.
The state health insurance plan, to which the vast majority of the population belongs, reimburses patients partially for any medicine, test or procedure prescribed.
Juppe said in the television interview that the government would not curtail the right of doctors to prescribe one or two anti-biotics for a cold "but four or five is just too much".
He insisted the government "had a medical view of the situation and not just an accountant's view".
